The word Tycoon comes from the Japanese word　大君　 (Dai - kun) [big - you]. The big character is simply that - big. The "you" character is a little more than just a simple "you". It's more closely related to "Mister - Mr" but located as a suffix. However it has an age stipulation and will be used by an older person to a younger. But, women will use it for men when they are in friendly terms. The example is Tanaka-san would change to Tanaka-kun. Many anime use this word.

So Dai-kun ends up basically meaning - the "big" dude. Or chopping off the big part and end up with "the dude".

So how did this get mixed up the American English for Tycoon?

Not really sure and I'm gonna do some guess work here since my Shogun era Japanese isn't that good. I'm thinking that with Perry's black ships the Americans finally got access to Japan where the Portuguese and Dutch were stuck to a small man-made off Nagasaki. Which is on the opposite of Japan from Tokyo. The Americans saw all these Japanese with retainers and looking important. So they asked who is he? That's the dude! The sailors coming back to the then started to associate the Japanese loan word to Carnegie and Rockefeller and because Japan didn't have a Roman alphabet at the time the word was spelled out like the heard it -- Ty-coon, Tycoon.

I think that there was a misunderstanding because modern Japanese post Shogunate Japan and more recently post WWII just doesn't have that word in circulation. It might have been an Edo (now known as Tokyo) thing. Or just a word that was used a fad.

Today the word that most closely associates with Dai-Kun is 親分 (oya-bun) [parent-part]. Which is loose translates to "father part" -- "father figure" -- "the boss". Which is a leader figure in the Yakuza, it can even be used all the way up to our favorite movie -- The GodFather and Don Corleone. But he'd be the Oya-Bun.

So where does this lay, legally speaking? As in what specific statute/law would she have broken here?

18 USC 793 (The Espionage Act)

Basically, giving any type of classified information to any persons, actor, or state who does not have authorization (clearance) is breaking this statute, and constitutes espionage in the eyes of U.S. Law.

The only real exception is that if it is done by mistake AND reported promptly, there seems to be provision that would not be prosecuted.

So, as we have already established, Clinton did move classified information to a private server and allowed non-cleared persons to view (violating Part D).

She claimed she didn't understand the classification system, and therefore this might fall under Part F. She most certainly was grossly negligent in that she moved classified information to an authorized location where it was viewed by unauthorized persons, even if it was "all just a big mistake".

Therefore the law then asks if she reported the error promptly.

The answer is NO. It was not until she was subpoenaed that she produced any emails and not until the FBI interviewed her as part of the investigation that she fully admitted to having done so. The fact that there are literally thousands of emails marked classified or containing classified info, sent over a period of time throughout her tenure as S.O.S. shows that she never intended to report.

Therefore, by moving and holding classified information on a non-secure, non-authorized server, allowing non-cleared, non-authorized persons to view and otherwise handle this information, and failing to report this promptly, she violated the statues of the Espionage Act.

Many whistleblowers have been prosecuted under this very statute and labeled as treasonous by those close to the government. Calling out Clinton as being guilty of treason was a way to equate her to them in order to illustrate the unequal prosecution of the law.

As I said in my opening, I think calling it Treason kind of muddies the water here, but it does show how the U.S. Justice System prosecutes laymen differently than those in positions of great power.
